prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many atoms are interrogated at a magic wavelength, opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single prize part for B009 with Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. I opened with B018 and ranked B009 sixth because I weight new states of matter, so I owe the committee a clear account of why I now lead with it. The case rests on a distinct physical idea, trapping many atoms at the magic wavelength so that the lattice light shift cancels for the clock transition, giving a Doppler- and recoil-free regime together with the statistics of thousands of atoms. It is verified in the way I care about most: independent Sr, Yb and Hg clocks at RIKEN, JILA, NIST, PTB and SYRTE agree at the 1e-18 level, and the systematic shifts (blackbody radiation, lattice hyperpolarizability, collisional and many-body shifts) are understood quantitatively. Several of these shifts are many-body and electronic-structure problems, so theory and experiment close on each other, which is the standard I apply to my own field. I would word the citation around the lattice concept and many-atom interrogation and keep both the 1e-18 figure and the redefinition of the second out of the operative text. The redefinition has not happened and is a consequence, not part of the discovery, which is Pearce's point and one I accept. The 1e-18 figure is a result of the invention and would make the citation sound like a prize for accuracy in general, which the 2005 and 2012 prizes already honoured. After reading all eight round-1 files and the chair's questions I found no new argument that favours another configuration over this one.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for ion control and ion clocks is the main reservation, and I am less relaxed about 2012 than about 2005. The lattice clock needs the comb for readout, and the 2012 citation already speaks of ultra-precise spectroscopy and clocks. A critic can call this a third prize in one metrology lineage. I have not seen a departure from known physics, so the prize would honour a new instrument regime and not a discovery about nature, which is exactly why I ranked it sixth at the opening. I also cannot rule out that a careful priority history would show that Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto or PTB have claims that two names cannot cover. If the overlap or the credit question were to turn out worse than the members who know the field expect, my reserve is B018, but that candidate carries its own problems: the 2016 topological-phases prize and the missing Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit.

responses.point: Pearce asks whether Jun Ye's decisive contribution is the lattice clock itself or the wider JILA programme, and says the redefinition of the second is a consequence that the citation should not depend on.
responses.response: I agree on the redefinition and have removed it from my citation. On Ye I read the record as separable: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first realisation, while Ye's group took the strontium lattice clock to record accuracy and stability and opened the many-body spin-exchange side. The latter is a statement about the lattice clock and not only about the broader JILA programme, since the density and collisional shifts that limited the clock are the physics that group worked out. I would still ask the outside experts to confirm that sequence, and Hall's 2005 role does not change my reading, because his prize honoured the comb and not the lattice clock. I would not lean on the JILA programme in the citation, only on the lattice clock.

responses.point: Johansson notes that no departure from known physics has been seen, so a clock prize rewards a record-setting instrument more than a discovery, and he sees overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: This was my own objection at the opening and I take it seriously. What moved me is that the lattice clock is a new regime of controlled many-body quantum matter as well as a better clock. Millimetre-scale gravitational redshift across a single sample and many-body shifts are measurements of physics that earlier clocks could not reach, even though they have not found new physics. Nobel citations have honoured such enabling regimes before, and I would rather the committee be explicit that it is rewarding that than pretend there is a discovery of new physics. I agree with Johansson that the credit may not stretch to Lemonde, Ludlow and Oates under the three-name limit, and I would put that to the reviewers as an open question, not claim it is settled. Because I leave Johansson's preferred B008 out of my configuration, his recusal question does not bear on my position.

responses.point: Mehlig, who also ranked B009 sixth at the opening, asks whether the committee can argue the lattice clock is a conceptual step beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes and not better engineering, and worries a widely expected prize can crowd out less familiar work such as B005.
responses.response: We started from the same position and I think the answer is yes for the concept, because magic-wavelength trapping is a principle and not a refinement of combs or ion traps. The test I would set is whether the citation could be written without the words precision or accuracy and still stand. It can: the invention is the magic-wavelength lattice, and I would state that. On crowding out, a prize being widely expected is not a scientific objection, and I would not penalise it for that. I do accept that B005 has had little attention here, and I defer to Mehlig and Kroll on the unsettled exponents. Where I differ is that I would not hold B009 back for a candidate whose flocking-transition exponents are only partly confirmed.

responses.point: Lindroth states that within the atomic community the magic-wavelength priority is not seriously contested as Katori's, and that the Katori and Ye roles are separable, though she says she is recalling the history from memory.
responses.response: That is the statement I most want to rely on, since I know the priority history only from reading. I find it consistent with what I understand of the sequence, in which Katori's proposal and early demonstration come before the accuracy race, but the committee should treat it as a member's recollection and ask for an independent check of who demonstrated what first. If an outside reviewer finds Lemonde or Takamoto have a stronger claim, I would revisit the credit before the final ballot. I also agree with her doubt that B010 or B001 pairs with the clock as a second part under the three-name limit, so I do not propose one.

uncertainties: How much weight the committee gives the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes on novelty; I give 2012 more than 2005 and cannot settle it from my own field.

Whether an independent priority history supports a two-name credit that leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Oates, Takamoto and PTB; my view rests on Lindroth's recollection and my own reading, not on a check.
Whether a prize for a new measurement regime, with no departure from known physics yet seen, meets the committee's standard for discovery.

If B009 were set aside, I am not sure which reserve I would put first: B018 has the 2016 overlap and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang gap, and B019 the missing Cao credit and an unsettled superconducting mechanism.
statement.conflict_note: No personal tie to Katori, Ye or any other credited name for B009 appears in my profile. I am a theorist in electronic structure and magnetism, not an atomic-clock specialist, and I defer to Lindroth, Kroll and Olsson on the atomic physics. For the reserve candidates B018 and B019 I have only scientific closeness through electronic-structure theory, and no personal connection to the credited names. I was Chair for the 2025 prize and have no stake in any of these candidates from that role.
